story.name: ジョニーの たび
story.title: Pie on Route Sixty-Six
story.line: ジョニーが さばくの ダイナーの はなしを します
story.ja: ロサンゼルスに着いたジョニーは、トラック運転手のアールの車に乗せてもらい、砂漠を東へ。ネオンの光るダイナーで、だれのことも hon と呼ぶウェイトレスのダーリーンに会う。おかわり自由のコーヒー、アイスをのせたチェリーパイ、満天の星。チップのことも教わる。最後にダーリーンが、メイン州で灯台守をしている兄の話をする。

segments.en: On the fourth night, Bunnie came early with a basket of snacks, and Redd showed up late, claiming he just happened to be walking by.
Don't mind me, I'm just passing through. Is that a story I hear? I love a good story. Especially a free one.
Gulliver cleared his throat. The ship from Japan, he said, took him all the way across the Pacific to the port of Los Angeles.
Los Angeles is a lovely place, but everyone's in a car. A sailor without a car is a sailor without legs.
Lucky for him, a truck driver named Earl was having breakfast at the port. Earl was heading east with a load of watermelons and wanted some company.
Earl didn't talk much. But when he did, it was worth waiting for. He said, the desert's got two speeds, son. Slow and slower.
They drove for hours. The city turned into hills, and the hills turned into desert, with mountains far away that never got any closer.
By the time the sun went down, they were on an old highway, the famous one, Route Sixty-Six. And up ahead, there was a light.
It was a neon sign, pink and blue, buzzing a little, with three big letters that said EAT. Under it was a small silver diner.
Ooh, I love those! The shiny ones, with the little stools that spin around? Please tell me it had the stools.
It had the stools. Red ones. I spun around on mine twice before Earl gave me a look.
Behind the counter was a waitress named Darlene, with big hair and a pencil behind her ear. She called everybody hon. Earl, Gulliver, even the cook.
She poured Gulliver a cup of coffee before he even sat down. And every time the cup got half empty, she came back and filled it up again.
I asked her, how much for the refills? And she said, hon, it's bottomless. I almost cried. That's my favorite word in English.
Bottomless, huh? Free refills? Now that's what I call a business model. I've got to get in on that.
Earl ordered the meatloaf. Gulliver asked Darlene what was good, and she leaned in and said, the cherry pie, hon. Trust me.
It came warm, with a scoop of vanilla ice cream melting slowly down the side. Pie à la mode, Darlene called it.
I'll tell you something. I've had pepper buns in Taipei and sugar on snow in Vermont. That pie was right up there with them.
In a booth, a family on a road trip was arguing about the Grand Canyon. The kids wanted to see it. The dad wanted a bed.
Earl turned around on his stool and told them, it's just a big hole in the ground. But it's a big hole you've got to see.
When it was time to pay, Gulliver counted out exactly what the check said. Earl shook his head and put a few more dollars on the counter.
He said, in this country, you tip, son. Darlene's on her feet all night. So I tipped. Generously. With my last few dollars.
Aw, that's so nice of you. So then what? You just got back in the truck and kept going?
Then we stepped outside, and I looked up. I've been at sea my whole life, and I have never seen so many stars.
There was no moon, and no city for a hundred miles. The sky was more stars than dark, and they could hear the neon sign humming.
Then Darlene came out with a coffee to go, for the road. She asked where Gulliver was headed, and he said he honestly had no idea.
And she said, well, hon, my brother keeps a lighthouse up in Maine, and he could use some help this winter. Interested?
A lighthouse, huh? Let me guess. You said yes before she even finished the sentence.
I said yes before she finished the word lighthouse. But that, my friends, is tomorrow's story. The last one.
Bunnie packed up the basket. Redd took the leftover snacks, for safekeeping, he said. And above the island, there seemed to be more stars than usual.

predict.ask: さいごの はなし、とうだいで なにが おこる？
choices: The lighthouse light breaks and he fixes it with a pie tin.
On a foggy night, he helps a lost fishing boat get home.
He finds his old compass in the lighthouse.
